The Intrinsic Value of a Watch – Part 1

Some of you may have seen the post with the $50 vs $500 watch (not my video). Others may have read my post on why, on a human level, watches are significant. This post will be more technical than either of the other posts but will still touch on the intangibles of watches that make them valuable works of art.

How a Quartz Watch Works and Why They Are Cheaper

If you have done any watch shopping, you probably have noticed that mechanical watches are something that generally you pay a high premium for. There are exceptions, such as Seiko, Orient, Sea-Gull, and other Chinese manufacturers. These low cost mechanical watches are great for first getting in to mechanicals, however there are reasons for their lower cost that I will touch on a bit later.

Certainly some of the high end brands produce expensive quartz watches. However, these are almost never a good value for the money. The reason for this is one of simple economics. Quartz movements are simply not very complicated in comparison to a mechanical watch. Yes, they are a feat of engineering skill, but it is on a different scale and for a different reason than a mechanical watch.

You see, the way a quartz watch works is via a concept known as piezoelectricity. Piezoelectricity means that when the object in question is stressed mechnically (such as squeezed, vibrated, folded, etc.), it gives off electricity. Additionally, when electricity is passed through the object, it will vibrate at a specific frequency. Quartz watches take advantage of this by having a battery pass a current through them (through a microchip), they vibrate at a specific frequency, which in turn is passed back into the microchip which turns this frequency into a regular, once a second electrical pulse. This pulse drives a tiny motor which turns the gears that move the hands on the watch’s dial. You can spot a quartz watch quite easily because the seconds hand will only move once a second (or if it has an LCD display, obviously).

This is certainly an engineering feat, particularly for the time when they first came on the market. However, economies of scale and rapidly advancing technology have reduced the cost of producing these quartz movements to $5 or less in most instances. Their microchips, while once considered advanced, are now incredibly commonplace and not all that interesting from a modern technical standpoint. Likewise with their little stepper motors.

So, when you pay for a quartz watch, you largely are paying for just the look of the watch, not what is inside. Sure, some high end brands have (and do) produce quartz watches, but when you buy one, recognize you are paying almost entirely for the brand name. There is no real history to quartz watchmaking as it emerged in the 1970s. Meanwhile, there are mechanical movements which have been in production largely unchanged for almost 200 years in some cases.

The Components of a Mechanical Watch

There are lots of places you could read about or watch videos of how a mechanical watch works, and I will link to a few at the end of the post. However, I will summarize the main components.

Power Source

The power source of a mechanical watch is not electric. Instead, on a hand wound watch there is a spring, called the mainspring. This mainspring is what stores the energy which drives a mechanical watch. As you turn the crown of a hand wound watch, the mainspring contracts. As the mainspring expands again, it turns the barrel. This barrel releases the energy to the gears.

Escapement

The escapement of a mechanical watch is the gear that turns a minimum of 5 times a second. The revolutions of the escapement are constrained by pallet jewels which lock and unlock the gears as the escapement turns. Jewels are used because of their low friction and durability. This prevents all the energy of the mainspring from being exhausted very quickly. As the escapement turns, it has a fork which pushes the balance wheel.

Balance Wheel and Hairspring

The escapement turns a wheel, called the balance wheel. The balance wheel in turn winds and unwinds the hairspring, often just called a balance spring. This regular motion is the heart of what allows a watch to keep time, in conjunction with the escapement. By winding and unwinding a regular interval we control how fast the gears are allowed to turn.

Gear Train

The gears of a watch are turned by the barrel. The gears are arranged such that the gearing ratio decreases at each gear. So the barrel will turn a gear that takes the longest amount of time to make a revolution, which turns a gear that makes multiple revolutions for each revolution of the first wheel, wheel in turn drives another wheel, etc. The last wheel is geared to the escapement. By attaching hands and gears to the gears of the gear train, we could measure time. In watches with “complications” such as the date, there are of course more wheels/gears needed to control these. At the end of the day though, all of these are being driven by the motion of the escapement, which derives its power from the unwinding in the mainspring.

Automatic Watches

Watches which are called “automatic” still have all these components. However, connected to the stem of the mainspring there is an unbalanced rotor. As you move your wrist, this rotor spins, winding the mainspring. Most automatics could also be wound by the crown, however this is not always the case. Seiko being the most notable exception on some of its lower end mechanical watches.

Summary

A quartz watch does away with most of these components. As a result, it actually is much easier to make an accurate quartz watch. If all you care about is what the watch looks like on the outside, and that it keeps time, a quartz is all you need. Of course, you won’t get a second hand that rotates smoothly such as that on a mechanical where the second hand is moving 5+ times a second. But that isn’t the only reason a mechanical watch is more valuable. Mechanical watches represent centuries of research and development, dating back to at least the 14th century. People who demand mechanical watches do so not because they are the most accurate, but because they are in some ways the most human. The top of the line watches (Jaeger LeCoultre, Patek Phillipe, etc.), beyond even Rolex, Omega, etc. are those which are produced (sometimes entirely, from creation of the movement to the case!) by hand. This adds an even greater human element to a watch, and imbues it with more history and a more prestigious pedigree.

In part 2 I will go more in depth on what separates one mechanical movement from another, and talk a little bit about historical significance of brands and why that has such an impact on what a watch costs.
